item.title: HET/VIRUS maps nickel and iron 85,000 km into the coma
item.description: Cochran and colleagues observed 3I/ATLAS on 2025 December 9 with the VIRUS integral-field spectrograph on the Hobby-Eberly Telescope, sampling the coma every 1,327 km out to about 85,000 km sunward. Alongside the usual cometary molecules the spectra show many very strong Fe I and Ni I lines, which the authors call an important difference from Solar System comets. The averaged log Q(Ni)/Q(Fe) is 0.19 (nickel about 1.5 times iron), similar to values Hutsemekers et al. report at comparable heliocentric distances. The radial profiles fit only if the gas flows out at about half the speed seen in Solar System comets at the same distance (0.3 km/s adopted). Biver et al. have proposed a heavy, CO2-rich gas as the cause, and the authors repeat that suggestion. Accepted in The Planetary Science Journal.

timeline_events.note: Abstract and HTML of 2609.01785 checked. v1 2026-09-01, accepted PSJ, 1,327 km sampling, ~85,000 km sunward, half-speed outflow, log Q(Ni)/Q(Fe)=0.19 all confirmed. Two fixes. (1) The paper compares the 0.19 to Hutsemekers et al. values 'for heliocentric distances comparable to our observations'. That reference covers the whole trajectory, so 'pre-perihelion' is the researcher's addition. (2) The CO2 link is Biver et al.'s suggestion, which the paper repeats, not the authors' own result. Also added the paper's own statement that the strong Ni I and Fe I lines are an important difference from Solar System comets.

item.title: Post-perihelion polarimetry: the extreme negative branch persists and deepens
item.description: Gray and colleagues extended polarimetry with FORS2 at the VLT, ALFOSC at the Nordic Optical Telescope and FoReRo2 at a 2 m telescope to phase angles of 1 to 30 degrees, the widest coverage obtained for any interstellar object. The unusual polarization survived perihelion unchanged in character, with the R-band minimum now pinned at -2.94% at 5.5 degrees phase and the inversion angle at 16.1 degrees. The curve matches small trans-Neptunian objects (Huya, Ixion, Varuna, 1999 DE9) and the Centaur Pholus, and at 30 degrees 3I is about 3.5 percentage points more polarized than typical high-polarization comets. Modelling favours porous aggregates larger than 10 microns built of weakly absorbing submicron grains, with a dust albedo near 0.7, about ten times that of 67P's dust.

timeline_events.note: 2609.04932 v1 2026-09-04. Table 2 gives R-band Pmin -2.94 +/- 0.03% at 5.52 deg and inversion 16.10 deg. Text: '3.5 percentage points' more than typical high-polarisation comets at 30 deg. Huya, Ixion, Varuna, 1999 DE9 and Pholus are named. Model: aggregates larger than 10 microns of submicron monomers, with geometric albedo ~0.7, 'an order of magnitude higher' than 67P. Instruments and the 1-30 deg range match the abstract.

item.title: Plasma-tail ions show 3I/ATLAS is nitrogen-rich
item.description: WEAVE integral-field spectroscopy on the William Herschel Telescope on 2025 November 30 and December 2 detected five ions in the anti-solar tail: N2+, CO+, CO2+, H2O+ and CH+. The N2+/CO+ ratio sets a lower limit of N2/CO > 0.023 +/- 0.001, which the authors call N2-rich compared to Solar System comets and similar to the few N2-rich comets measured. Rosetta's in-situ value for 67P was first ~0.006 and later revised to 0.03. NH2 is still undetected, which points to nitrogen stored as N2 rather than ammonia, the same pattern as C/2016 R2. The authors link it to cold formation conditions, near 20 K by the reasoning applied to 67P.

timeline_events.note: 2609.05393 v1 2026-09-04. The five ions, both dates, N2/CO > 0.023 +/- 0.001, the missing NH2 and the C/2016 R2 analog are confirmed. The comparison with 67P is misleading. The paper gives Rubin et al. 2015's ~0.006, then says Rubin et al. 2019 found 0.03 later in the Rosetta mission. That later value is the one plotted in its Figure 4, and it is above 3I's lower limit. 'About four times 67P' is dropped.

item.title: Astrochemical models: the extreme water D/H fits a metal-poor birth cloud
item.description: Furuya, Cordiner and colleagues ran gas-ice astrochemical models from molecular cloud to dense core to test whether the water D/H of about 0.01 in 3I/ATLAS fits the low-metallicity origin suggested by its carbon isotopes. Lower metallicity boosts deuteration of H3+ and its transfer into water ice; the observed value is most readily reproduced at half solar metallicity or below and cloud densities near 10^4 per cubic cm, provided the cosmic-ray ionization rate stays below 10^-15 per second. One solar-metallicity parameter set also exceeds 0.01, so low metallicity is favoured rather than required. Accepted in ApJ Letters.

timeline_events.note: 2609.12370 v1 2026-09-11, v2 2026-09-14, accepted ApJL. The abstract gives Z <~ 0.5 Zsun, n ~ 1e4 cm^-3 and zeta < 1e-15 s^-1. Section IV.1 confirms the one Z=1 parameter set above 0.01 (n=1e4, chi=10, zeta=1e-16). The H3+ deuteration mechanism is stated in the abstract.

item.title: JWST: water ice in the coma before and long after perihelion
item.description: Protopapa and colleagues report JWST NIRSpec spectra from 2025 August 6, 2025 December 22 and 2026 April 1, at 3.3, 2.4 and 5.7 AU from the Sun. A broad 3 micron water-ice band appears with weak or missing 1.5 and 2.0 micron bands. The best model is submicron-to-micron icy aggregates mixed with refractory material. The band was 77% deep in August and 94% deep in April, when a second population of larger ice-rich grains and a Fresnel-like feature consistent with crystalline ice appeared. The authors allow either crystalline ice at both epochs or a change from amorphous to crystalline. The December spectrum was not modelled because water gas, organics, Ni I emission and warm dust overlap the band, but the authors describe the band shape as largely unchanged between epochs. They place 3I at the refractory-rich end of a continuum running through Solar System comae and mid-sized trans-Neptunian objects.

timeline_events.note: 2609.19286 v1 2026-09-16, accepted ApJL. Dates, distances (3.3/2.4/5.7 AU), band depths 77% and 94%, weak 1.5/2.0 micron bands and refractory-rich aggregates are confirmed. Two fixes. (1) Section III.1 describes 'the 3I spectra' as showing a strong 3 micron band. Discussion says the band 'remains largely unchanged between epochs, supporting a common water-ice origin for the band both before and after perihelion'. So the December spectrum is contaminated, but it is not band-free. (2) The paper allows crystalline ice at both epochs as well as an amorphous-to-crystalline change, so 'crystalline ice appeared' overstates it.

item.title: Thermophysical model ties the late methane to cosmic-ray processing
item.description: Rawat and Acharyya coupled a nucleus thermophysical model to galactic cosmic-ray processing and ran 12,000 models against the measured H2O, CO, CO2 and CH4 production. The viable models start from a volatile-rich body formed below 20 K beyond the CO snowline and need an effective cosmic-ray exposure of 0.87 to 3.1 billion years. Radiation strips methane from near-surface layers and converts some CO into CO2, while methane trapped deeper in the water ice survives and is released once post-perihelion heating reaches it. The authors treat the pre-perihelion methane signal as a weak constraint because it is blended with ethane bands. Accepted in ApJ.

timeline_events.note: 2609.19694 v1 2026-09-17, accepted ApJ. The abstract gives 12000 runs, T < 20 K beyond the CO snowline, 0.87-3.1 Gyr exposure, CO converted to CO2 and CH4 depleted near the surface. Methods section: pre-perihelion CH4 is 'strongly blended with adjacent C2H6 bands' and treated as a weak constraint.

item.title: Indian telescopes: carbon chemistry turns typical after perihelion, nucleus about 0.55 km
item.description: Ahuja and colleagues monitored 3I/ATLAS after perihelion, from 2025 November 16, with the 0.5, 1.2 and 2.5 m Physical Research Laboratory telescopes, the 2 m Himalayan Chandra Telescope and a 0.132 m refractor. CN, C2 and C3 production rates and ratios moved from carbon-depleted before perihelion to carbon-typical after it, which they attribute to fresh subsurface material. Broadband colours (B-V 1.03, V-R 0.59) stayed nearly constant and consistent with pre-perihelion values. They are redder than the Sun and long-period comets and match ultrared-material-rich Solar System objects. The JPL non-gravitational acceleration, with an outflow speed halved per Biver et al., gives a mass of 4.85 x 10^11 kg from CO2 and 3.66 x 10^11 kg from water, and a nucleus radius of 0.45 to 0.65 km. Published in MNRAS 552.

timeline_events.note: 2609.22596 v1 2026-09-18, MNRAS 552 issue 3 (Nov 2026). The colours, the change from carbon-depleted to carbon-typical and the 0.45-0.65 km radius are confirmed. The full text gives two masses. The JWST CO2 production rates give (4.85 +/- 1.06) x 10^11 kg. The TRAPPIST OH-derived water gives (3.66 +/- 0.53) x 10^11 kg and radius 0.55 +/- 0.10 km. The radius range combines both. Both use JPL SBDB non-gravitational terms and Biver's halved outflow speed. The event quoted only one mass. The telescope list is also made complete.

item.title: Survey forecast: LSST may find 0 to 8 more comets like 3I/ATLAS in ten years
item.description: Albornoz-Montenegro and Fuentes model how the size distribution of interstellar objects sets detection rates in TESS, Pan-STARRS, ATLAS and Rubin's LSST, anchoring the comet population on the single ATLAS detection of 3I/ATLAS. They estimate about 0 to 8 detections of 3I-like comets by LSST in ten years and about one by TESS over its mission, independent of the nucleus size distribution. Fitting 1I/'Oumuamua and 3I/ATLAS from the same size distribution, they suggest planet formation ejects more asteroid-like bodies than comets. Submitted to A&A.

timeline_events.note: 2609.25488 v1 2026-09-21, submitted to A&A. The abstract gives ~0-8 3I-like comets by LSST in 10 years, ~1 by TESS, independent of the nucleus size distribution, and more asteroid-like than cometary objects. Figure 4 caption: the ATLAS-W68 detection rate is fixed at one, the empirical anchor.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): An independent inbound campaign (Santana-Ros et al., ApJ 1007, 182; arXiv:2608.18371) used Faulkes and Maidanak imaging from July to September 2025. It measured the sunward jet at a position angle of 278 +/- 2 degrees, consistent with Serra-Ricart's 280.7 +/- 0.2 degrees, the 279.5-degree plume of 2 July and Hubble's fan at 280 degrees. It found the jet stable over several months. The paper does not measure a period itself. It cites Serra-Ricart's 7.74-hour modulation as consistent with its own months-long stable jet. So the jet Loeb's geometry rests on is real, persistent and seen by separate teams, while the wobble still rests on one team's data. The paper places the source in a discrete active region at latitude about +75 degrees, citing ATel 17350. Taken at face value that is roughly 15 degrees from the pole, looser than the within-8-degrees placement behind the 0.5% figure, though both numbers are model-dependent.
item.rationale: Independent confirmation of the PA ~280 jet. The modulation is correctly attributed to Serra-Ricart, so the wobble is not double-counted. The latitude figure limits Loeb's 8-degree placement, model-dependent both ways.

case_updates.note: Confirmed: 2608.18371 (ApJ 1007, 182) measures its own jet PA of 278 +/- 2 deg. It cites Serra-Ricart's 280.7 +/- 0.2 deg, the 2 July plume at 279.5 deg and HST's 280 deg fan. Latitude ~+75 deg is cited from ATel 17350 (Oldani et al.). Error: the periodic PA modulation is not an independent detection. The body says Serra-Ricart and colleagues 'also detected a small periodic modulation of the jet PA with a period of 7.74 +/- 0.35 h'. The conclusion only says the stability, coupled with that modulation, is consistent with precession 'as suggested by Serra-Ricart'. Reworded so the paper is not credited with confirming the wobble.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): Post-perihelion polarimetry by the same team (Gray et al., arXiv:2609.04932), now covering phase angles 1 to 30 degrees, shows the anomaly survived perihelion: R-band minimum -2.94 +/- 0.03% at 5.52 degrees, inversion angle 16.10 degrees, with the negative branch deeper and shifted to smaller angles at longer wavelengths. At 30 degrees phase 3I is about 3.5 percentage points more polarized than typical high-polarization comets and about 2 points more than Hale-Bopp and 2I/Borisov, so the 'unprecedented among comets' reading holds with more data, not less. The closest matches remain small trans-Neptunian objects (Huya, Ixion, Varuna, 1999 DE9) and the Centaur Pholus, and the team's model needs porous aggregates of weakly absorbing submicron grains with a dust albedo near 0.7, about ten times that of 67P's dust.
item.rationale: Direct follow-up of the A-08 measurement: the anomaly is confirmed and slightly deepened, and the natural TNO-like reading is strengthened, both stated.

case_updates.note: Table 2 and the text of 2609.04932 confirm every figure: -2.94 +/- 0.03% at 5.52 deg, inversion 16.10 deg, wavelength trend, 3.5 p.p. above typical high-polarisation comets and ~2 p.p. above Hale-Bopp and 2I at 30 deg, the TNO and Pholus match, and albedo ~0.7. The paper itself says the polarisation of 3I 'exceeds that of other comets'. Does not duplicate the existing A-08 text.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): The post-perihelion polarimetry model (Gray et al., arXiv:2609.04932) sets a minimum particle size of about 10 microns, because smaller grains would have formed a bright anti-solar tail that its images do not show. That floor matches the characteristic size Loeb derived, and the paper credits independent studies finding a coma of relatively large grains. The model distribution then runs up to 1000 microns, into the millimetre range Loeb's bracket excludes. The authors also note that particle size has only a minor effect on polarisation and colour within that range, so the polarimetry supports the lower edge of the bracket but not the upper one. The natural reading in the same paper is porous clumps of submicron monomers with a dust albedo near 0.7, so a 10-micron particle need not be a solid grain. JWST spectra (Protopapa et al., arXiv:2609.19286) model the ice-bearing grains as submicron-to-micron aggregates, with larger micron-sized ones by 2026 April. That is a different population seen at a different wavelength, so the two results are not yet one size distribution.
item.rationale: Credits the ~10 micron floor that agrees with Loeb, gives the model's true 10-1000 micron range and states the polarimetry's weak size sensitivity.

case_updates.note: Misreading. The modelled size distribution in 2609.04932 runs from a 10 micron minimum to a 1000 micron maximum (power-law index -3.5). The paper adds that 'particle size has only a minor effect on the polarisation and colour within the considered range'. So the result does not land inside Loeb's 1-100 micron bracket. It extends to the millimetre sizes Loeb excludes, and the polarimetry barely constrains size. The 10 micron floor is set by the missing anti-solar tail (confirmed in the text).

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): Post-perihelion integral-field spectra from the Hobby-Eberly Telescope on 2025 December 9 (Cochran et al., arXiv:2609.01785, accepted PSJ) show many very strong Fe I and Ni I lines across tens of thousands of km of coma, so by December the iron was plainly present. Nickel still led: the averaged log Q(Ni)/Q(Fe) is 0.19, about 1.5 to 1, similar to values reported at comparable heliocentric distances. A separate team summarising the literature (Ferellec et al., arXiv:2609.05393) calls the Ni/Fe ratio of 3I larger than what is usually measured for Solar System comets. It cites post-perihelion values that match pre-perihelion ones at similar distance. The HET authors call the strong metal lines an important difference from Solar System comets, and exceptional even against 1I and 2I. The fitted parent scale lengths are only about 3,000 km and could be shorter. The authors note that surface temperatures there are too low to vaporise metallic iron or nickel. They conclude the atoms either come straight off the nucleus in metallic form or come from a very short-lived parent, the second being the carbonyl-type route already in this case.
item.rationale: Closes the 'without iron' premise for the post-perihelion period. Credits that Ni still exceeds Fe, that the ratio stays above Solar System norms, and that the observers call the metal lines exceptional. Gives both readings the paper offers.

case_updates.note: Ferellec's literature line is quoted accurately: 'a Ni/Fe ratio larger than what is usually measured for solar system comets'. log 0.19 is confirmed. Fixes: (1) Cochran compares to Hutsemekers et al. 'for heliocentric distances comparable', not specifically pre-perihelion. Ferellec separately cites Hoogendam et al. for post-perihelion matching pre-perihelion. (2) The researcher left out both of the paper's readings of the short parent scale length. Cochran says the metals 'must' come 'directly off the nucleus in their metallic form or must have a very short-lived parent'. It also notes surface temperatures are too low to vaporise metallic Fe or Ni, and that 3I was exceptional even against 1I and 2I for its strong Ni I and Fe I. Both points belong in a case built on this anomaly.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): The 'nitrogen-depleted' premise behind the ratio argument now needs a refinement. WEAVE spectra of the plasma tail (Ferellec, Opitom & Snodgrass, arXiv:2609.05393) set N2/CO > 0.023 +/- 0.001. The authors call that N2-rich compared to Solar System comets and similar to the few N2-rich comets measured, while NH2 stays undetected. So the nitrogen is not missing: it is held as N2 rather than ammonia. A reservoir that favours N2 would plausibly leave less nitrogen for HCN too, raising CH3OH/HCN without any methanol excess. That link is an inference here, not a result of the paper. The analog the authors name is again C/2016 R2, the native comet that already beats 3I on methanol. Limits both ways: N2/CO is a lower limit derived from ions, and an N2-rich reservoir speaks to the denominator, not to the sunward methanol enhancement.
item.rationale: The N2-rich, NH3-poor result bears on A-26's argument that CH3OH/HCN is high because HCN is scarce, and names the same C/2016 R2 analog. The misleading 67P multiple is removed.

case_updates.note: The N2/CO limit, missing NH2 and C/2016 R2 analog are confirmed, and the HCN step is properly flagged as inference. Error: 'about four times the in-situ value at 67P' uses Rubin 2015's ~0.006. The paper itself reports Rubin 2019's later 0.03, which exceeds 3I's lower limit and is the value in its Figure 4.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): Astrochemical modelling by Furuya, Cordiner and colleagues (arXiv:2609.12370, accepted ApJL) finds the water D/H of about 0.01 is most readily reproduced in a birth cloud at half solar metallicity or below, with density near 10^4 per cubic cm. Lower metallicity enhances deuteration of H3+ and its transfer into water ice. At half solar the match needs a narrow corner of parameter space. At one fifth solar, the lowest value modelled, the allowed range is broader. This bears on Loeb's mass-budget objection in a specific way: the D/H points to a metal-poor cloud, but the grid does not test far lower metallicities, so it cannot say how metal-poor. It also cuts against the paper's own reading: one solar-metallicity parameter set also exceeds 0.01, so the D/H favours low metallicity rather than proving it.
item.rationale: Tests the natural-origin inference behind A-25's D/H number. States the model grid's true range (Z = 1 to 0.2) and the paper's own exception.

case_updates.note: The figures are confirmed, but 'they allow much lower values' goes past the paper. The grid runs only from Z=1 down to Z=0.2. Section IV.1 says the D/H is reproduced 'in a restricted region of parameter space' at Z=0.5 and over a broader one at Z=0.2. The 'bears on Loeb's mass-budget objection' line is kept, with a statement of what it can and cannot settle.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): JWST NIRSpec spectra at three epochs (Protopapa et al., arXiv:2609.19286, accepted ApJL) show the coma's water-ice signature did not end in December. The broad 3 micron ice band was 77% deep on 2025 August 6 at 3.3 AU and 94% deep on 2026 April 1 at 5.7 AU outbound. By April a second population of larger ice-rich grains had appeared. JWST's own spectrum of 2025 December 22, days after the SPHEREx re-observation, was not modelled because water gas, organics, Ni I emission and warm dust overlap the band, and no depth is given. The authors nonetheless describe the band shape as largely unchanged between epochs and argue for a common water-ice origin before and after perihelion. That sits uneasily with an ice signature that had mostly vanished, though JWST's small aperture samples only the inner coma while SPHEREx sees the whole of it. Either way the disappearance at the core of this case was temporary at most.
item.rationale: Shows the 'disappearance' is temporary or aperture- and epoch-specific, and reports the paper's own statement about band continuity, which bears on the December result in both directions.

case_updates.note: Depths, dates and the second grain population are confirmed. The claim that JWST 'neither confirms nor contradicts' SPHEREx understates the paper. Section III.1 describes 'the 3I spectra' (all three in Fig. 1) as showing a strong 3 micron band. Epoch 2 is excluded from modelling because of contamination 'across the 3 um water-ice absorption region'. Discussion says the band morphology 'remains largely unchanged between epochs, supporting a common water-ice origin for the band both before and after perihelion'. That is relevant tension with SPHEREx's December disappearance. It is qualified because the December depth was never quantified, and JWST's small 7x7-pixel aperture differs from SPHEREx's.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): A thermophysical model with cosmic-ray processing (Rawat & Acharyya, arXiv:2609.19694, accepted ApJ) reproduces the late methane across 12,000 runs. Radiation destroys methane in the outer layers and converts some CO into CO2. Methane trapped deeper in water ice is released only after perihelion heating reaches it. The viable runs need formation below 20 K beyond the CO snowline and an effective exposure of 0.87 to 3.1 billion years. This treats the out-of-order release as a real effect that a simple sublimation sequence does not give. The limits: the fit cannot separate dust content from exposure. The independent SOHO/SWAN water reductions it fits against disagree by about one to two orders of magnitude (the paper gives both figures). It also notes methane was weak or undetected inbound, with the pre-perihelion feature blended with ethane bands, and uses it as a weak constraint rather than a clean detection or a firm absence.
item.rationale: A dedicated model of the A-22 puzzle, with its stated limits, including one that touches how firm the inbound absence of methane is.

case_updates.note: The model content is confirmed. Two wording fixes. (1) The paper treats the pre-perihelion CH4 feature as 'a weak constraint rather than as a direct CH4 detection', and its introduction says methane 'remained weak or undetected' inbound. 'Rather than as a clean non-detection' inverts the emphasis. (2) The paper gives the SWAN discrepancy as 'nearly an order of magnitude' in one place and '1-2 orders of magnitude' in another, so both are reported.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): A non-gravitational mass estimate by Ahuja et al. (arXiv:2609.22596, MNRAS 552) uses the same equation as Loeb's floor: mass equals outgassing momentum divided by acceleration. It uses the measured JPL non-gravitational terms rather than an upper limit. With JWST CO2 production rates it gives (4.85 +/- 1.06) x 10^11 kg. With water production from OH it gives (3.66 +/- 0.53) x 10^11 kg, and the radius is 0.45 to 0.65 km. That is roughly 70 to 90 times below the 33-billion-ton floor and within a factor of two to three of Loeb's post-perihelion revision to about 1 billion tons, so his revised figure and these agree in order of magnitude. Every estimate of this kind scales directly with the assumed gas outflow speed. Ahuja adopts the speed Biver et al. measured with IRAM, about half the usual value, and the HET/VIRUS coma profiles (Cochran et al.) independently fit only at that halved speed.
item.rationale: New masses from the same physics Loeb used, each correctly tied to its gas species. Credits his revised figure and states the shared dependence on outflow speed.

case_updates.note: Wrong pairing. 2609.22596 gets (4.85 +/- 1.06) x 10^11 kg from the JWST CO2 production rates (Cordiner; Belyakov). The (3.66 +/- 0.53) x 10^11 kg comes from water, via TRAPPIST OH. 'Two teams now put that speed near 0.3 km/s' is also loose. Biver et al. (IRAM) measured it, and Ahuja simply adopts Biver's halved relation. Cochran could not measure velocity with VIRUS but finds profiles fit only at half speed. The arithmetic is otherwise sound: 3.3e13 kg / 3.66e11 = ~90, and 1e12 / 3.66e11 = ~2.7.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): A survey forecast (Albornoz-Montenegro & Fuentes, arXiv:2609.25488, submitted to A&A) still expects Rubin's LSST to find about 0.2 to 100 interstellar objects per year, mostly asteroid-like. For comets like 3I, which it anchors on the single ATLAS detection, it predicts only about 0 to 8 in ten years, and it reads its results as planet formation ejecting more asteroid-like bodies than comets. So 'Rubin will find many more' holds for interstellar objects in general, but 3I-like comets are expected to stay rare. That makes the population question testable: several more 3I-like comets would weaken the rarity point Loeb makes, while none would sit inside the forecast without settling it. Separately, a non-gravitational estimate puts the nucleus radius at 0.45 to 0.65 km (Ahuja et al., arXiv:2609.22596).
item.rationale: Quantifies the 'Rubin will find many more' line separately for ISOs in general and for 3I-like comets, and states what each outcome would and would not show.

case_updates.note: The forecast figures are confirmed. Balance fix: the same paper predicts LSST will find ~0.2-100 ISOs per year in total, so 'Rubin will find many more' (ISOs generally) is not tempered. Only the 3I-like comet class is, and the paper reads its numbers as more asteroid-like than cometary ISOs being produced. Zero detections in ten years is inside the 0-8 forecast, so it would be consistent with the model rather than a separate win for Loeb. The rarity framing is softened to match.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): Broadband photometry on both sides of perihelion shows the dust colour itself stayed red: a stable reddish colour with no secular change from July to September 2025 (Santana-Ros et al., arXiv:2608.18371), and after perihelion B-V 1.03 and V-R 0.59, constant through the run and consistent with pre-perihelion values (Ahuja et al., arXiv:2609.22596). The blueness in this case is therefore confined to the near-perihelion coronagraph window. That fits the gas-emission explanation, and the same post-perihelion data show C2 and C3 recovering from carbon-depleted to carbon-typical, but it also fits the timing in Loeb's reading, so it narrows the event without settling it.
item.rationale: Brackets the perihelion blue colour with red, stable dust colours before and after, which constrains when and how the blueness happened.

case_updates.note: 2608.18371 abstract: 'stable reddish color with no significant secular variation' July-September 2025. 2609.22596: B-V 1.03, V-R 0.59, 'nearly constant' and 'consistent with the reported pre-perihelion values', from 2025 Nov 16 on. Carbon-depleted to carbon-typical is confirmed. The bracketing inference is fair and states both readings.

item.text: the unusual polarimetric properties of 3I persist across perihelion
item.speaker: Zuri Gray et al. (abstract)
item.context: Abstract of the post-perihelion polarimetry paper, bearing on A-08: the extreme negative polarization was not a one-epoch effect.

quotes.note: The abstract of https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04932 reads 'reveal that the unusual polarimetric properties of 3I persist across perihelion and match recent independent post-perihelion observations'. The quoted fragment matches character for character, and the date 2026-09-04 is v1.

findings.item: 2608.18371 (Santana-Ros et al.) bears on more than A-05. Its jet PA of 278 +/- 2 deg independently matches Serra-Ricart's 280.7 +/- 0.2 deg and reports the periodic PA modulation, so the existing 2026-08-18 event should add A-16 (and A-15) to relates_to. Its dust model (90% organics, 10% pyroxene aggregates) fits the pre-perihelion polarimetry (A-08), and its stable red colour bears on A-11. It is now published: ApJ 1007, 182.

All dates used are the arXiv v1 submission timestamps (UTC) from each abstract page: 2609.01785 Sep 1; 2609.04932 Sep 4; 2609.05393 Sep 4; 2609.12370 Sep 11 (v2 Sep 14 fixed an abstract typo); 2609.19286 Sep 16; 2609.19694 Sep 17; 2609.22596 Sep 18; 2609.25488 Sep 21. The public listing usually appears the next weekday.

Publication status from the abstract pages: 2609.01785 accepted PSJ; 2609.12370 accepted ApJL; 2609.19286 accepted ApJL; 2609.19694 accepted ApJ; 2609.22596 MNRAS vol 552 issue 3 (Nov 2026); 2609.25488 submitted to A&A; 2609.04932 and 2609.05393 have no journal listed.

Shared systematic for A-01/A-10/A-12: two independent results put the 3I gas outflow speed near 0.3 km/s, half the solar-system norm (HET/VIRUS Haser fit in 2609.01785; IRAM 0.37 km/s at 1.36 AU from Biver et al., as cited in that paper). Every momentum-based mass (M = Q m u / J) scales linearly with u, which lowers Loeb's 33-billion-ton floor and mainstream masses by the same factor. It does not change the ratio between them.

Caveat for A-06: 2609.19694 states that independent reductions of the SOHO/SWAN water data differ by 1-2 orders of magnitude depending on the Lyman-alpha inversion assumptions. A-06's official text quotes a single SWAN figure (~3.2e29 molecules/s) with no such caveat.

Possible correction for A-22's observation text ('no CH4' pre-perihelion): 2609.19694 says the pre-perihelion CH4 feature in Belyakov et al. (ApJ 1001, L11) is blended with C2H6 and treats it as a weak constraint, not as a direct detection or a clean non-detection. Worth reading Belyakov et al. before the console calls the pre-perihelion absence firm.

The N2-rich result (2609.05393) maps to no existing case, and none of these papers puts forward a proponent claim about it. I did not create a case, to avoid tally inflation. It goes into A-26 (the HCN-denominator argument) and the timeline only. It also strengthens A-07's existing counter-reading that CN is the denominator, but only by inference. C/2016 R2 is again the closest native analog, as it already is for methanol in A-26.

A-08's observation still correctly quotes the pre-perihelion values (-2.7% at 7 deg, inversion ~17 deg). Post-perihelion R-band values are -2.94 +/- 0.03% at 5.52 +/- 0.30 deg with inversion at 16.10 +/- 0.06 deg (Table 2 of 2609.04932). The shift is attributed to better small-phase coverage, not to evolution.

2609.22596 also reports a spin-period periodogram: global minimum at 12.81 h, with a local minimum at 16.61 +/- 0.02 h consistent with earlier 16.16-16.79 h reports. It is ambiguous, so I left it out of the case text. 2609.25488 adopts D = 0.44 km as the lower size limit for 3I.

None of the nine papers mentions Loeb, technosignatures or artificial origin. Every case update above sets the paper's natural reading next to what it credits or limits in the claim. No new_claims were filed because this batch contained no proponent statements.

missing: Gray et al., Multi-Wavelength Post-Perihelion Polarimetry of 3I/ATLAS (2026-09-04): minimum about -2.9% at 5.5 deg, no evolution across perihelion, modelled as moderately porous aggregates of weakly absorbing submicron monomers giving dust much BRIGHTER than typical comets, which conflicts with Choi et al.'s dark dust. Bears on A-08; also a timeline candidate if no other batch covers it. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04932

Protopapa et al., JWST Reveals Refractory-Rich Water Ice in 3I/ATLAS (2026-09-16, accepted ApJL, ApJL 1011 L11): NIRSpec on 2025 Aug 6, Dec 22 and 2026 Apr 1 shows a strong 3 micron water-ice band with weak or absent 1.5/2.0 micron bands, explained as refractory-rich ice aggregates, plus a second population of larger ice-rich grains in April 2026. Directly complicates A-20's 'ice signature disappeared'; sci.news covered it 2026-10-26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19286

Ferellec et al., Ion abundances in the plasma tail show 3I/ATLAS is N2-rich (2026-09-04): WEAVE-LIFU on 2025 Nov 30 and Dec 2 gives N2/CO > 0.023, N2-rich compared with Solar System comets. Needed to correct the 'nitrogen-poor' framing in the A-26 update. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05393

Furuya et al., High water D/H of 3I/ATLAS consistent with a low-metallicity origin (2026-09-11, accepted ApJL): observed D/H most readily reproduced at 0.5 solar metallicity or below. Bears on A-25 alongside Hopkins et al. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12370

Rawat et al., Delayed Methane Detection in 3I/ATLAS: GCR-Driven Subsurface Stratification (2026-09-17, accepted ApJ): 12,000 thermophysical runs favour formation below 20 K beyond the CO snowline and a cosmic-ray exposure of 0.87-3.1 Gyr that converts CO to secondary CO2. A second, independent cosmic-ray age alongside Barry-Taylor, bearing on A-06 and A-25. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19694

Ahuja et al., Post-perihelion Photometric and Spectroscopic Monitoring of 3I/ATLAS (2026-09-18, accepted MNRAS): composition moved from carbon-depleted pre-perihelion to carbon-typical post-perihelion; nucleus radius 0.45-0.65 km from the non-gravitational force. The radius bears directly on the A-10 mass-fraction caveat. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22596

Aravind et al. report an unusually high, or in another passage typical, CN/OH ratio for 3I. Not mapped by the researcher, yet it bears on A-07's 'depleted denominator' counter-argument for Ni/CN and on A-26's HCN-deficit reading: CN does not look depleted relative to water. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26577

Belyakov et al. v2, JWST/MIRI Finds ISM-like Amorphous Silicates (accepted ApJL, v2 2026-09-16): the first MIRI silicate result, which the researcher names only in findings. The console has no silicate entry, and this paper plus Thomas et al. 2610.37540 should be presented together, with Thomas's olivine-versus-pyroxene caveat. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27535

item.title: Hobby-Eberly traces 3I's gas to 85,000 km: it flows out at half speed
item.description: Cochran et al. observed 3I/ATLAS on 2025 December 9 at 2.03 au with the VIRUS integral-field spectrograph on the Hobby-Eberly Telescope, sampling the coma every 1,327 km out to about 85,000 km sunward. The Haser model fits only if the gas expands at about 0.30 km/s instead of the canonical 0.597 km/s. That matches earlier radio velocities from IRAM (0.37 km/s at 1.36 au) and ALMA (0.345 km/s for CO and 0.276 km/s for HCN at 2.4 au). The spectra also show many very strong Fe I and Ni I lines, with log Q(Ni)/Q(Fe) = 0.19 and very short parent scale lengths. The authors cite Biver et al.'s suggestion that heavy CO2-rich gas is what slows the flow. Published in PSJ 7, 226; sci.news covered it on 2026-10-05.

timeline_events.note: All numbers check out against arXiv 2609.01785: 1,327 km sampling, about 85,000 km, 0.30 vs 0.597 km/s, IRAM 0.37 km/s at 1.36 au, ALMA 0.345/0.276 km/s at 2.4 au, log Q(Ni)/Q(Fe)=0.19. The sci.news page (Natali Anderson) confirms PSJ 7, 226. Two fixes. The sci.news date is 2026-10-05, not 2025-10-05. And the heavy-CO2 explanation is Biver et al.'s suggestion, which Cochran et al. cite; they do not propose it themselves.

item.title: VLT/UVES: a severe ammonia deficit sets 3I apart from Solar System comets
item.description: Aravind et al. (accepted in A&A) followed the coma with VLT/UVES from August 2025 at 3.14 au to February 2026 at 4.34 au. NH and NH2 are strongly depleted. The C2/CN ratio shows carbon-chain depletion and drifts with distance, which the authors read as a coma effect such as hyperactivity, not a change in composition. Water production rises steeply, with a heliocentric index of 8.47 +/- 0.23. In abundance-ratio space 3I sits outside the canonical Solar System comet cluster. It is nearest the strongly carbon-chain-depleted comets, including the Giacobini-Zinner type, but more depleted in NH and C3 relative to CN, and its unusually high CN/OH ratio sets it apart from that group as well. The authors read this as formation in an exceptionally cold natal environment.

timeline_events.note: The numbers check out against arXiv 2609.26577: 3.14 au in Aug 2025, 4.34 au in Feb 2026, water index 8.47 +/- 0.23, NH/NH2 strongly depleted, G-Z comets as the nearest analogue. Two fixes. 'Outside the comet family' overstates the result: the paper says 'outside the canonical Solar System comet cluster' and calls 3I an extension of known comet diversity. The researcher also left out that the authors give the unusually high CN/OH ratio as what sets 3I apart from G-Z-type comets, and that they put the C2/CN drift down to coma effects such as hyperactivity rather than compositional change.

item.title: Ammonia as a metallicity clock: 3I's parent star was metal-poor
item.description: Hopkins, Bannister, Bitsch, Lintott and Forbes combined a chemical partition model with APOGEE DR17 stellar abundances and found that an interstellar object's ammonia content tracks its parent star's metallicity. Ammonia was not measured directly, so they inferred 3I's NH3/H2O as about 0.001 or less, roughly an order of magnitude below Solar System comets. From that they place its parent star at [Fe/H] between -0.8 and 0.0, which corroborates the velocity- and isotope-based ages by an independent route. The same model predicts 3I should be CO2-poor, the opposite of what was observed. The authors call this inconsistent with observations, offer cosmic-ray conversion of CO to CO2 as a possible explanation, and say it is unclear whether that could work while CO stays at ordinary levels. They also note giant planets are rare around metal-poor stars, so 3I was probably ejected by another mechanism such as a stellar flyby.

timeline_events.note: Checked against arXiv 2609.30827 v1 (posted 2026-09-25, submitted to AJ). The [Fe/H] range, the CO2-poor prediction and the flyby inference are all in Sections IV.1 and IV.3. Two precision fixes. The NH3/H2O of 0.001 or less is an adopted input, not a measurement: the paper says ammonia production was not measured directly for either ISO, and derives the value in Appendix A. And the authors do not leave the CO2 mismatch fully unexplained: they offer cosmic-ray conversion of CO to CO2 as a possible explanation and say it is unclear whether that can work while CO stays at ordinary levels.

item.title: Near-opposition polarimetry: the deep negative branch holds, but the dust may be dark
item.description: Choi et al. measured polarization with the 1.6 m Pirka Telescope down to a phase angle of 0.70 degrees. Their fit to the combined post-perihelion curve gives a minimum of -3.04 +/- 0.028% at 5.98 degrees and an inversion angle of 16.3 degrees. That agrees with Gray et al.'s post-perihelion -2.94% at 5.52 degrees, which Gray et al. attribute mainly to better small-phase coverage than in the first -2.7% fit, not to dust evolution. The branch persisted across perihelion. A visible-to-mid-infrared energy distribution from HST, VLT, SPHEREx and JWST gives dark dust with an effective albedo of about 0.04, a size index of 3.0 to 3.3, and a minor amorphous-silicate component. Dirty water-ice models fail to reproduce the thermal emission. The polarimetry favours a highly porous scattering structure. Gray et al. also favour porous aggregates, but of weakly absorbing grains that make the dust brighter than in typical comets, so what makes the branch this deep is still open.

timeline_events.note: The figures check out against arXiv 2610.04919: 1.6 m Pirka, 0.70 deg, -3.04 +/- 0.028% at 5.98 deg, inversion 16.3 deg, albedo about 0.04, q=3.0-3.3, a minor amorphous silicate component, dirty-ice models failing, highly porous. 'Deeper than the first -2.7% report' needs the context the paper gives: the fit is consistent with Gray et al.'s post-perihelion -2.94%, and Gray et al. attribute the difference from -2.7% mainly to better small-phase coverage, not to dust evolution. The researcher also missed a real disagreement. Gray et al. (arXiv 2609.04932) model the curve with weakly absorbing monomers, i.e. dust much brighter than typical comet dust, while Choi et al. find dark dust. The two teams agree on porosity, not on brightness.

item.title: Mass-loss audit revised: gas alone took 0.4 to 1.25% of the nucleus
item.description: Frincke and Seligman's third version (accepted by MNRAS) integrates every published 3I production rate into a gas-only mass loss of 1.83 to 5.77 x 10^10 kg, about 1.7 to 5.2 m of surface, or 0.40 to 1.25% of the initial mass for an assumed 1.3 km radius and 0.5 g/cm3 density. Adding dust at dust-to-gas ratios of 1 to 4 raises the loss to roughly 3.7 x 10^10 to 3.0 x 10^11 kg and erosion beyond 10 m. The authors present all figures as lower limits; earlier versions gave 0.10 to 1.13% (May) and 0.12 to 0.53% (July).

timeline_events.note: Checked against arXiv 2606.01377 v3 (2026-10-12, accepted MNRAS). Gas-only loss is (1.83-5.77)e10 kg; the abstract gives 1.71-5.24 m and 0.40-1.25% for R0 = 1.3 km and 0.5 g/cm3. D/G=1 gives 3.72e10 kg and D/G=4 gives 2.98e11 kg. The authors present the figures as lower limits. Earlier versions: v1 (2026-05-31) gave 0.10-1.13%; v2 (2026-07-22) gave 0.12-0.53% (its own text also says 0.12-0.51%). The paper itself says the result depends strongly on the assumed radius, and names Thoss et al.'s smaller radius as one that would raise it.

item.title: ZTF catches a short-lived icy-grain halo and a blue outer coma
item.description: Liu, Zhang, Liu and Hui (ApJL 1008, L26) used ZTF imaging to estimate dust mass-loss rates of about 123 to 203 kg/s before perihelion and 596 to 1,412 kg/s after. In late November 2025 the outer coma was anomalously blue and steeply fading, and that structure was gone by 2026 January 18. They model it as icy grains of 5 to 10 microns with about 0.1% absorbing carbon, destroyed over a projected length of 6.4 to 7.2 x 10^4 km.

timeline_events.note: Every figure is in the arXiv 2610.21206 abstract and text: 123-203 and 596-1412 kg/s; a blue outer coma on 2025 Nov 29, gone by 2026 Jan 18; destruction length (6.4-7.2)e4 km; 5-10 micron icy grains with f_C about 0.1%. ApJL 1008, L26 is confirmed.

item.title: Keck and Gemini publish a ten-month benchmark record of 3I
item.description: Bolin et al. report 14 imaging and 8 spectroscopic optical epochs plus near-infrared data from 2025 July to 2026 May. Colours stay red and unchanged across perihelion (g-r = 0.732 +/- 0.029), and activity falls faster outbound (Afrho proportional to r^-3.34) than it rose inbound (r^-2.10). Dust speeds imply 2.7 x 10^9 to 1.0 x 10^10 kg of 1 micron to 1 mm grains lost, a 0.26 to 0.99 m global layer. The compact sunward feature seen beside an antisolar tail on 2025 August 27 weakened through September. C2/CN nearly doubled, from 0.257 to 0.481, and no water-ice absorption survives their calibration tests.

timeline_events.note: Checked against arXiv 2610.32972 (2026-10-23). The abstract gives 14 imaging and 8 spectroscopic epochs, g-r = 0.732 +/- 0.029, Afrho indices -2.10 and -3.34, 2.7e9 and 1.0e10 kg, 0.26 and 0.99 m, and C2/CN from 0.257 to 0.481. The body text says the compact sunward feature 'weakens through September as the tail strengthens'. The paper reports no robust water-ice absorption.

item.title: Second JWST/MIRI study: 3I's silicates are almost entirely amorphous
item.description: Thomas et al. took a JWST/MIRI low-resolution spectrum on 2025 December 16 at 2.21 au. They found a smooth 10-micron silicate feature unlike those of Solar System comets, best fitted by amorphous pyroxene (pyroxene to olivine about 180:1). The best-fitting crystalline fraction is zero with a 5.3% upper limit, in line with Belyakov et al.'s 3.1% from MIRI medium resolution, and a 6.83-micron feature points to aliphatic C-H material. The authors conclude the dust saw little thermal processing, while noting that diffuse interstellar dust is olivine-type, so this is not a simple interstellar-medium match.

timeline_events.note: Checked against arXiv 2610.37540 (2026-10-27). The observation date is 2025 Dec 16 at 2.21 au. The paper gives pyx/ol about 180:1, best-fitting crystalline fraction zero with a 5.3% upper limit, Belyakov et al.'s 3.1%, and a 6.83 micron aliphatic C-H feature. Its discussion says diffuse ISM dust is olivine-type, rather than the pyroxene type seen in 3I and Solar System comets.

item.addition: Update (Sep-Oct 2026): Four papers approach the CO2 excess from different sides. Cochran et al. (Hobby-Eberly/VIRUS) find the coma gas leaving at about 0.30 km/s, half the speed expected near 2 au, in line with IRAM and ALMA radio velocities, and cite Biver et al.'s suggestion that heavy CO2-rich gas is the cause. Barry-Taylor models galactic cosmic rays converting CO into CO2 toward a laboratory equilibrium CO/CO2 of about 0.1. Fitted to 3I's measured ratios, the model gives an initial CO/CO2 of about 1.5 and an age of at least 0.6 Gyr, which supports processing as the source of the extra CO2 and formation outside the CO ice line. Aravind et al. (VLT/UVES) find water estimated from forbidden oxygen lines exceeding the OH-based value except near perihelion, which they read as CO2 feeding the coma chemistry. One limit cuts against the natural reading. Hopkins et al.'s chemical model correctly recovers 3I's metal-poor origin from its ammonia, yet the same model predicts 3I should be CO2-POOR compared with Solar System comets. The authors call this inconsistent with observations. They also say it is unclear whether cosmic-ray processing could raise CO2 that far while keeping CO at ordinary levels. The size of the CO2 excess is still not fully explained.
item.rationale: Four papers bear on the CO2-dominance case: a cosmic-ray age model that supports the official explanation, a slow outflow attributed to CO2, an oxygen-line comparison, and a stated open inconsistency in the natural model (Hopkins et al.), which meets the framing rule's call for limits that cut against the official reading.

case_updates.note: The A-06 content is accurate, but two details need fixing. Cochran et al. cite Biver's heavy-gas suggestion rather than making it their own. Hopkins et al. say it is 'unclear' whether cosmic rays could do this, which is softer than 'doubt'. Barry-Taylor's 0.1 equilibrium comes from laboratory work (Pilling et al.), and the paper reads its result as supporting formation outside the CO ice line. The existing official_explanation already cites cosmic-ray processing (arXiv:2510.26308), so the update now reads as an extension of it rather than a new idea.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): Low-resolution integral-field spectra from the Hobby-Eberly Telescope on 2025 December 9, at 2.03 au, show many very strong Fe I and Ni I lines together. The averaged log Q(Ni)/Q(Fe) is 0.19, so nickel is about 1.5 times iron, close to the high-resolution values at similar distances. By this stage iron is present at comparable abundance. The measured parent scale lengths are very short. The authors conclude the metals leave the nucleus directly in metallic form or come from a very short-lived parent, even though the surface is far too cold to vaporize metallic iron or nickel. The high-resolution teams reached the same conclusion, and the release mechanism is still open. Credit where due: the same authors call 3I exceptional in Fe and Ni even compared with 1I and 2I. Before this century Fe I and Ni I had been seen only in the sungrazers of 1882 and 1965. Better instruments have since found them in many ordinary comets (Manfroid et al.), but there the lines are relatively weak and show only at high spectral resolution, while in 3I they are strong enough to stand out in a low-resolution spectrum.
item.rationale: An independent post-perihelion Ni/Fe ratio and parent scale lengths bear directly on the nickel-without-iron argument; the authors concede the release mechanism is unresolved and state how unusually strong the lines are.

case_updates.note: The figures check out against arXiv 2609.01785 (log ratio 0.19, short parent scale lengths, surface too cold for metallic Fe/Ni, exceptional compared with 1I and 2I). One credit the researcher dropped: in the same passage Cochran et al. stress that the Fe/Ni lines Manfroid et al. found in ordinary comets are 'relatively weak' and visible only at high spectral resolving power. 3I's lines, by contrast, are very strong even at low resolution. That point supports the claim side and belongs in the update under the framing rule.

item.addition: Update (Oct 2026): The deep branch has held up and is now measured more precisely. Choi et al. added Pirka polarimetry down to a 0.70 degree phase angle. Their combined post-perihelion fit gives a minimum of -3.04 +/- 0.028% at 5.98 degrees, with inversion at 16.3 degrees. Gray et al.'s post-perihelion campaign found -2.94% at 5.52 degrees and no significant change across perihelion, and attributes the step from the first -2.7% mainly to better coverage at small phase angles. The ice-rich explanation offered early on (30-40% water ice by volume) no longer carries the result alone: Choi et al.'s dirty-ice models fail to reproduce the thermal spectrum. Both teams now favour porous dust aggregates, but they disagree on the dust itself. Choi et al. find dark, absorbing dust with an effective albedo of about 0.04 and a size index of 3.0 to 3.3, inside the Solar System comet range. Gray et al. model weakly absorbing submicron grains that make the dust much brighter than in typical comets. Why 3I's branch is so deep is still an open modelling question.
item.rationale: New data confirm and sharpen the measured minimum and weaken the ice-only part of the official explanation; the two modelling teams' disagreement on dust brightness is stated rather than smoothed over.

case_updates.note: Two problems. First, the claim that Gray et al. found 'ice alone could not match the polarization and colour together' is not in Choi et al. or in the Gray et al. post-perihelion abstract (arXiv 2609.04932), so it comes out. Second, the 'present natural reading' is not settled. Gray et al. model the branch with moderately porous aggregates of weakly absorbing submicron monomers, which makes the dust BRIGHTER than typical comet dust. Choi et al. find DARK dust (albedo about 0.04). 'The anomaly has grown stronger' also overstates the change: the move from -2.7% to about -3% is attributed to better small-phase coverage, not to a change in the dust.

item.addition: Update (Oct 2026): The mass loss has now been totalled from every published production rate. Frincke and Seligman (MNRAS, v3) find a gas-only loss of 1.83 to 5.77 x 10^10 kg, or 0.40 to 1.25% of a 1.3 km nucleus. Including dust at dust-to-gas ratios of 1 to 4 raises it to roughly 3.7 x 10^10 to 3.0 x 10^11 kg. They present these as lower limits. Taken at face value, this is far below the tenth-to-sixth of the mass Loeb said the early acceleration demanded. Two limits cut the other way. First, as the authors themselves note, the percentage depends strongly on the assumed radius. Against the 1.6 x 10^11 kg nucleus that Thoss, Loeb and Burkert derived from the acceleration, the same gas mass would be roughly 11 to 36%. That figure is this console's division of the two published numbers, not a published result, and an independent radius of 0.45 to 0.65 km from the non-gravitational force (Ahuja et al.) points the same way. Second, Cochran et al. measure the coma gas expanding at about 0.30 km/s, half the usual speed. The console's reading, not tested in any paper, is that slower gas carries less momentum per kilogram, which would make the rocket-effect budget tighter rather than looser. The coma expansion speed is only a proxy for the speed at which gas leaves the surface.
item.rationale: Directly tests Loeb's mass-loss argument against measured production rates, and records genuine caveats that favour the claim: the radius dependence, which the authors flag, and the slow outflow, labelled as console inference.

case_updates.note: The Frincke figures and the 11-36% arithmetic (1.83e10 and 5.77e10 divided by 1.6e11) are correct. Frincke et al. themselves say the result depends strongly on the initial radius and that Thoss et al.'s smaller radius would raise it, so that caveat can be credited to the paper. The momentum point, though, is the console's own reasoning, not a published result. The Haser coma expansion speed is only a proxy for the speed at which gas leaves the surface, and no paper in this window recomputes the thrust budget with it. Label it, as the 11-36% figure is labelled. A post-perihelion MNRAS paper also derives a 0.45-0.65 km radius from the non-gravitational force (arXiv 2609.22596), which supports the small-radius side.

item.addition: Update (Oct 2026): Loeb's estimate of about 10 million kg of dust shed (about 3.3 kg/s) rested on a single grain size. Measured budgets that use size distributions come out much larger. Liu et al. (ZTF) find 123 to 203 kg/s before perihelion and 596 to 1,412 kg/s after, roughly 40 to 400 times his rate. Bolin et al. (Keck/Gemini) derive 2.7 x 10^9 to 1.0 x 10^10 kg over 2025 July to 2026 May for grains of 1 micron to 1 mm, a global layer only 0.26 to 0.99 m thick on a 1.3 km nucleus. With that size range the budget does not become implausible, which undercuts the mass-budget reason for excluding millimetre grains. But the 1 mm upper cutoff is an assumption that their images do not constrain. Credit to the bracket itself. Bolin et al. note that the MIRI spectra favour 10 to 100 micron grains, close to Loeb's own range. Choi et al.'s energy distribution needs grains down to about 1 micron, while the morphology points to a minimum near 10 microns for the dust that shapes the large-scale coma. The measured ejection speeds, Liu's 190 m/s times a^-1/2 (a in microns) and Bolin's 0.9 to 1.2 m/s perpendicular for 145 micron grains, describe slow large grains, as both Loeb and Jewitt require.
item.rationale: Three independent dust budgets and grain-size constraints test the premise of the dust size paradox, with the assumed upper cutoff stated and the part of Loeb's bracket that holds credited.

case_updates.note: Four fixes. (1) 'Hundreds of times larger' is not uniform. ZTF's pre-perihelion 123-203 kg/s is about 40-60 times Loeb's 3.3 kg/s; Bolin's 2.7e9-1.0e10 kg is about 270-1,000 times his 1e7 kg. (2) Bolin et al. state their adopted 1 mm upper size cutoff 'is unconstrained by our images', so 'include millimetre grains' is an assumption, not a measurement. That weakens 'the mass-budget exclusion does not stand'. (3) Bolin's speed at 145 microns is 0.9-1.2 m/s perpendicular (sunward models 2.1-6.6 m/s), not simply 'roughly 1.2 m/s'. (4) A credit was missed: Bolin et al. note that MIRI favours 10-100 micron grains, which is close to Loeb's own bracket.

item.addition: Update (Oct 2026): ZTF photometry gives the disappearing ice a measurable lifetime. Liu et al. find a fading coma component, read as icy grains of 5 to 10 microns with about 0.1% absorbing carbon, destroyed over a projected 6.4 to 7.2 x 10^4 km. Its amplitude fell from about 1.9 to 0.4 between 2025 November 25 and December 20. That fits the SPHEREx picture of icy grains sublimating away after perihelion. Bolin et al.'s Gemini near-infrared spectra from 2025 September and December show no robust water-ice absorption, capping 10 micron pure-ice grains at about 1-3% of the inner-coma scattered light at 1.20 microns. The authors say this is compatible with the earlier detections, which sampled different epochs and coma regions. A limit on the 'ice vanished' reading: JWST/NIRSpec (Protopapa et al.) still saw a strong 3 micron water-ice band on 2025 December 22 and again on 2026 April 1. The 1.5 and 2.0 micron bands, by contrast, were weak or absent, which the authors model as ice mixed into refractory-rich aggregates. The ice signature faded at some wavelengths and in some parts of the coma, not everywhere.
item.rationale: Independent constraints on the transient icy-grain component bear on the vanishing-ice case, including a JWST post-perihelion ice detection that complicates both sides' simple story.

case_updates.note: The Liu figures check out (amplitude 1.9 to 0.4 between 2025 Nov 25 and Dec 20). Bolin's 1-3% limit at 1.20 microns for 10 micron pure-ice grains is verified. But the researcher misreads Bolin et al. as reporting an inconsistency. Their text says the earlier ice detections 'sample different epochs and regions' and that 'an icy population that contributes little to our inner-coma continuum remains allowed', i.e. the results are compatible. The researcher also missed Protopapa et al. (JWST/NIRSpec, accepted ApJL, arXiv 2609.19286): a strong 3 micron water-ice band on 2025 December 22 and 2026 April 1, carried by refractory-rich ice aggregates. That bears directly on the SPHEREx 'ice mostly disappeared' observation in A-20.

item.addition: Update (Sep-Oct 2026): More lines of evidence point to an old, cold, metal-poor origin. Hopkins et al. infer a parent-star [Fe/H] of -0.8 to 0.0 from 3I's ammonia deficit (inferred NH3/H2O of about 0.001 or less), a route independent of kinematics and isotopes. Furuya et al.'s astrochemical models reproduce the high water D/H most readily at metallicities of half solar or below. Aravind et al. read the extreme NH and carbon-chain depletion as formation colder than even the most depleted Solar System comets. Thomas et al. find the silicates almost entirely amorphous (crystalline fraction at most 5.3%), meaning little thermal processing. Barry-Taylor's cosmic-ray age method gives at least 0.6 Gyr with a flat likelihood beyond that, which is consistent with 10-12 Gyr but does not measure it. One point bears on Loeb's mass-budget objection and is not resolved. Hopkins et al. note giant planets are rare around metal-poor stars, so 3I was probably ejected by another route such as a stellar flyby. They argue that one flyby-ejected object among three known ISOs suggests the route is common, but give no number for how much material metal-poor systems release that way, and that supply is exactly what Loeb disputes.
item.rationale: Age and composition results from the window corroborate the natural reading, and one stated implication touches the premise of the mass-budget argument; the authors' own qualitative claim is reported alongside its limit.

case_updates.note: Two fixes. (1) Hopkins et al. do address how common flyby ejection is, qualitatively: 'Having just one example ... out of the three ISOs discovered so far suggests that ejection by stellar flyby is a common mechanism.' The update should say so rather than only 'does not quantify it'. (2) The NH3/H2O value is inferred, not measured. Missed: Furuya et al. (accepted ApJL, arXiv 2609.12370) find 3I's high water D/H is most readily reproduced at metallicity of 0.5 solar or below, which bears directly on this case.

item.addition: Update (Sep 2026): The nitrogen side of the ratio is more complicated than 'nitrogen-poor'. VLT/UVES spectra (Aravind et al.) show NH and NH2 strongly depleted from 3.14 au inbound to 4.34 au outbound. Hopkins et al. infer 3I's NH3/H2O at about 0.001 or less, roughly an order of magnitude below Solar System comets. Aravind et al. also cite Biver et al.'s finding that HCN/H2O was depleted at 1.37 au, though they note their own CN/OH ratio is typical. Meanwhile ion spectra of the tail (Ferellec et al.) give N2/CO above 0.023, making 3I N2-RICH compared with Solar System comets. The nitrogen is there; it sits in N2 rather than in ammonia and possibly HCN. A shortage of HCN relative to methanol would still raise CH3OH/HCN without any methanol excess. But the denominator argument now rests on a hydride deficit, not on a general lack of nitrogen, and the typical CN/OH weakens it.
item.rationale: A-26's counter-argument rests on the HCN denominator; new papers quantify the hydride depletion but also show 3I is N2-rich and CN/OH typical, which both sides need.

case_updates.note: 'Nitrogen-poor coma' is wrong as a blanket statement. Ferellec et al. (arXiv 2609.05393, WEAVE-LIFU tail spectra, 2025 Nov 30 and Dec 2) find N2/CO greater than 0.023, i.e. 3I is N2-RICH compared with Solar System comets. The depletion is in nitrogen hydrides (NH3, and HCN per Biver et al.), not in nitrogen overall. Also, Biver's HCN depletion is cited here through Aravind et al., and those authors add that the CN/OH ratio they measure is typical, which cuts against a simple HCN-deficit reading. Both points belong in A-26, since its counter-argument rests on the denominator.

item.addition: Update (Oct 2026): A second, independent route to a blue coma has been documented after perihelion. ZTF colour profiles on 2025 November 29 show an anomalously blue outer coma at large radii, gone by 2026 January 18, while the inner few thousand km stayed red (g-r = 0.63). Liu et al. attribute it to a short-lived population of icy grains fading as they sublimate. Keck/Gemini colours show no significant change across perihelion in the inner coma (Bolin et al.). A limit: both data sets are a month or more after the late-October coronagraph measurement. They show a natural mechanism for transient blueness but do not re-test the perihelion colour itself.
item.rationale: Directly addresses an observed blue colour, with an explicit limit on how far it reaches.

case_updates.note: Checked against arXiv 2610.21206 (blue outer coma on 2025 Nov 29, gone by 2026 Jan 18; inner g-r = 0.63 +/- 0.01 over (1-5)e3 km) and 2610.32972 (no significant colour change across perihelion). The stated limit, that both data sets come after the coronagraph epoch, is appropriate.

item.claim: A paper published last month showed 3I/ATLAS lost only between 0.04% and 1.25% of its total mass, retaining over 99% despite strong non-gravitational acceleration, which violates comet dynamics because you cannot get that much propulsive force while shedding almost no material.
item.assessment: The paper is real and the upper figure is accurate: Frincke and Seligman v3 (2026-10-12, accepted MNRAS) gives 0.40 to 1.25% of the initial mass from gas alone. The auto-caption renders the lower bound as '.04%'; the paper's figure is 0.40%, and no version contains 0.04% (v1 0.10 to 1.13%, v2 0.12 to 0.53%). The authors call their figures lower limits. Adding dust at the measured dust-to-gas ratios of 1 to 4 raises the loss to roughly 3.7 x 10^10 to 3.0 x 10^11 kg, about 0.8 to 6.5% of a 1.3 km nucleus (console arithmetic). The 'over 99% retained' framing depends entirely on that assumed 1.3 km radius, which the paper itself flags. Against the 1.6 x 10^11 kg nucleus Thoss, Loeb and Burkert derived from the acceleration, the same gas would be roughly 11 to 36% (console arithmetic). Credit to the claim: the coma gas was measured expanding at half the usual speed (Cochran et al.). In this console's reading, which no paper has tested, that would mean less thrust per kilogram and make the rocket-effect budget harder, not easier.

new_claims.note: The transcript (20261101-ihnlxrNdhEQ.txt) is auto-captioned and reads 'a pitiful. 04%', which is ambiguous. Saying the speaker misread 0.40 as 0.04 asserts more than the caption shows; say the paper's figure is 0.40% and no version contains 0.04%, which I confirmed for v1, v2 and v3. 'Several percent' with dust also needs fixing: 3.72e10 to 2.98e11 kg against a 1.3 km, 0.5 g/cm3 nucleus (about 4.6e12 kg) is roughly 0.8 to 6.5% (console arithmetic). The 'half speed means less thrust per kg' point is console reasoning and should be labelled as such.

item.claim: Hobby-Eberly data forced astronomers to assume 3I's gas flows at exactly half the speed of normal comets, about 0.3 km/s instead of 0.6 km/s, a fluid-dynamics failure that rewrites cometary velocity and suggests gas bound to a nanomachine swarm or dragged by a magnetic tail.
item.assessment: The numbers are accurate: Cochran et al. (arXiv 2609.01785, PSJ 7, 226) could fit the VIRUS profiles only with an outflow of about 0.30 km/s against a canonical 0.597 km/s at 2.03 au. It was not an arbitrary patch: the same slow speeds had been measured directly by radio months earlier (IRAM 0.37 km/s at 1.36 au; ALMA 0.345 km/s for CO and 0.276 km/s for HCN), and the Haser model takes velocity as an input, so changing it is routine. The authors found the coma reasonably symmetric, which a uniform slow outflow fits without a magnetic tail. Limit on the official side: the heavy-CO2 explanation is offered as a suggestion, and no paper in this window shows quantitatively that CO2 loading reproduces the factor of two. No case currently covers expansion speed; it belongs inside A-06 (CO2) and A-10 (momentum budget) rather than in a new case.

new_claims.note: The transcript (20261017-5Gt9Soc0m4I.txt) matches the claim: 0.6 vs 0.3 km/s, 'radical arbitrary adjustment', and a magnetic tail dragging the gas. The assessment's figures match arXiv 2609.01785: 0.597 vs 0.30 km/s, IRAM 0.37 km/s at 1.36 au, ALMA 0.345 (CO) and 0.276 (HCN) km/s, 'the coma morphology is reasonably symmetric'. The authors do say they could not fit the data with nominal velocities and that 'something is different for 3I', and the assessment credits the official side's limit fairly.

item.claim: Until recently telescopes had only detected vaporized iron and nickel in comets during extreme sungrazing events like the Great Comet of 1882 and Ikeya-Seki in 1965, yet 3I shows a hyperdense concentration of them at over two AU.
item.assessment: Accurate as a paraphrase of Cochran et al.'s own introduction: before this century Fe I and Ni I had been seen only in those two sungrazers, and the authors call 3I exceptional in Fe and Ni even compared with 1I and 2I. The same paragraph adds context that cuts both ways. Manfroid et al. later found Fe and Ni in many ordinary Solar System comets far from the Sun, which A-07 already carries. But those lines are relatively weak and show only at high spectral resolution, whereas 3I's are very strong even at low resolution, so the claim's point about intensity stands. Cochran et al. find Ni about 1.5 times Fe (log ratio 0.19), so iron is present by December 2025. They agree the metals must come straight off the nucleus or from a very short-lived parent, a mechanism nobody has yet pinned down, since the surface is far too cold to vaporize metallic iron or nickel.

new_claims.note: The transcript matches. The assessment is accurate but one-sided. It cites the Manfroid sentence as an omission by the claim, yet the next clause of the same paragraph in Cochran et al. says those ordinary-comet lines are 'relatively weak' and visible only at high spectral resolving power. That supports the claim's 'hyperdense' point that 3I's lines are unusually strong. Under the framing rule, add that credit.

item.claim: 3I's negative polarization plunges to -2.7% at 7 degrees with an inversion angle of 17 degrees, while ordinary comets rarely dip below -1.5% and invert at 22 to 23 degrees.
item.assessment: The 3I figures are accurate for the pre-perihelion discovery paper (-2.7% at 7 degrees, inversion at 17.1 degrees), which calls the combination unprecedented. The comparison is slightly off: that paper gives a typical Solar System comet inversion angle of 20 to 22 degrees, not 22 to 23, and the -1.5% figure could not be traced to it. Later data make the point stronger, not weaker. Choi et al. (2026-10-04) fit a minimum of -3.04% at 5.98 degrees with inversion at 16.3 degrees, and Gray et al. found the branch unchanged across perihelion. The mechanism is not settled. Dirty-ice models fail to reproduce the thermal emission, so ice alone no longer carries the explanation. Both teams favour porous dust aggregates, but Choi et al. find dark dust with an ordinary comet albedo of about 0.04, while Gray et al. model weakly absorbing grains that make it brighter than typical comet dust.

new_claims.note: The transcript (20260910-VCnfmj04nXM.txt) matches. The -2.7% at 7 deg and about 17 deg are correct (Gray et al. 2025: 17.1 +/- 0.1 deg). But the comparison figures were not checked. The discovery paper gives typical Solar System comet inversion angles of 20-22 deg, not 22-23, and I found no '-1.5%' figure in it. 'The ice-rich explanation does not work alone' should be tied to its basis (dirty-ice models fail Choi et al.'s thermal fit). The two modelling teams also disagree on dust brightness.

item.claim: For weeks there was no conventional dust tail, all material pointed toward the Sun, and the fine dust simply was not there, a dust distribution physically impossible for a natural comet.
item.assessment: Largely right about the early morphology. Dust dynamics and the absence of a prominent antisolar tail imply that the dust shaping the large-scale coma had a minimum size near 10 microns (as cited by Choi et al.), and the early images were dominated by a sunward feature. The weeks were limited, though: Bolin et al.'s Gemini imaging already shows an antisolar tail on 2025 August 27 beside the compact sunward feature, which then weakened through September as the tail strengthened. 'Zero fine particulate matter' is not established either way for the early weeks. The fine dust that Choi et al.'s infrared energy distribution requires (grains of about 1 micron, size index 3.0 to 3.3) comes from data taken around December 2025, after perihelion. It shows small grains were present then, not that they were present in August. Large slow grains dominating the early optical morphology is a known behaviour of distantly active comets, so the distribution is unusual but not physically impossible.

new_claims.note: There is an epoch mismatch. The researcher counters an EARLY-morphology claim (the first weeks, July to August 2025) with Choi et al.'s energy distribution, which is built from observations 'around 2025 December', post-perihelion. That does not show fine dust was present in the early weeks. The Bolin et al. tail on 2025 Aug 27 is correctly cited (2610.32972 text: tail at PA 105 deg alongside a compact sunward feature confined to the inner coma). Choi et al. cite the 10 micron minimum for the dust dominating large-scale morphology.

item.text: Interestingly, this prediction is inconsistent with observations
item.speaker: Hopkins, Bannister, Bitsch, Lintott & Forbes (paper)
item.context: Their metallicity model, which recovers 3I's metal-poor origin from its ammonia deficit, predicts a CO2-poor 3I; the observed CO2 is similar to or above Solar System comets. This is a mainstream team stating an open problem in the natural model.

quotes.note: The quote matches character for character at arXiv 2609.30827v1 HTML, Section IV.1: 'Interestingly, this prediction is inconsistent with observations'. Speaker, date and context are accurate.

findings.item: Window search: three arXiv API queries (abs:"3I/ATLAS", all:"3I" AND interstellar, all:"C/2025 N1", plus a generic interstellar-object query), all sorted by submittedDate. They found no 3I/ATLAS paper posted 2026-10-25 to 2026-11-01 other than 2610.38485 (excluded) and 2610.37540 (in this batch).
findings.note: My export.arxiv.org query (abs:"3I/ATLAS", by submittedDate) also returns only 2610.38485 and 2610.37540 for 2026-10-25 to 2026-11-01. The same query shows several in-window 3I papers outside this batch (listed under missing), which may belong to another batch.

Version history: v1 2026-05-31 gave 0.10-1.13%, v2 2026-07-22 gave 0.12-0.53%, v3 2026-10-12 gives 0.40-1.25% of initial mass (gas only, R0 = 1.3 km, density 0.5 g/cm3, 1.83-5.77e10 kg). The video's '0.04%' is a misreading of 0.40%. No version says 0.04%. Cite the abs URL and say v3.

But the transcript is an auto-caption reading '. 04%'. Report it as 'renders the lower bound as 0.04%', not as a confirmed misreading by the speaker.

findings.item: Gas outflow velocity: the source is Cochran et al., arXiv 2609.01785 (posted 2026-09-01), published PSJ 7, 226 (doi 10.3847/PSJ/aea086). sci.news covered it 2026-10-05 (author Natali Anderson). Figures: 0.30 km/s adopted against a canonical 0.597 km/s at 2.03 au. IRAM gave 0.37 km/s at 1.36 au; ALMA gave 0.345 km/s (CO) and 0.276 km/s (HCN) at 2.4 au. This paper also falls in the September window, so it may arrive from another batch: de-duplicate.
findings.note: arXiv 2609.01785 was posted 2026-09-01. sci.news is dated Oct 5, 2026, by Natali Anderson, and cites PSJ 7, 226, doi 10.3847/PSJ/aea086. The velocity figures are verified.

findings.item: No existing case covers coma gas expansion speed. Recommend carrying it inside A-06 (CO2 as the slowing agent) and A-10 (momentum per kg in the rocket-effect budget) rather than opening a new case, per the tally-inflation rule.

A-08 numbers: the shipped -2.7% at 7 deg / inversion ~17 deg was correct for the pre-perihelion fit and should not be overwritten. Newer fits: -3.04 +/- 0.028% at 5.98 deg, inversion 16.3 deg (Choi et al. 2610.04919), and -2.94 +/- 0.03% at 5.52 deg (Gray et al. 2026, as cited by Choi, attributed to better small-phase coverage rather than dust evolution).

Mild inconsistency to avoid overstating: the 2026-08-18 timeline event says light-scattering modelling matches DENSE aggregates. Choi et al. and Gray et al. (as cited) favour HIGHLY POROUS aggregates. The console should not present grain structure as settled.

findings.item: Silicates: the console has no silicate content yet. Thomas et al. (2610.37540) is the second MIRI result after Belyakov et al. (2606.27535, 'ISM-like amorphous silicates', accepted ApJL, v2 2026-09-16). Thomas et al. find pyroxene-dominated dust and point out that diffuse interstellar dust is olivine-type, so do not echo 'ISM-like' without that caveat.

findings.item: The 11-36% figure in the A-10 update and the mass-loss claim is console arithmetic: Frincke gas mass 1.83-5.77e10 kg divided by the Thoss/Loeb/Burkert mass 1.6e11 kg (arXiv 2603.15735). Label it as derived if shipped.

Barry-Taylor (2610.04050) also gives total radius loss of 6-70 m when dust is included (cited by Frincke v3), against Frincke's 1.7-5.2 m from gas alone. The age result is a lower bound (>= 0.6 Gyr, flat likelihood above), not a measurement.

findings.item: Hopkins et al. (2609.30827) state an open problem for the natural model: their chemistry predicts a CO2-poor 3I, but observed CO2/H2O is similar to or above Solar System comets. This is useful for the owner's framing rule.
Nothing in this batch changes the Loeb scale value.

Quotes were limited to one short verbatim line by the copyright policy this agent runs under. Other candidates can be taken from the abs pages cited: the Cochran HTML section on outflow velocity, and the Choi and Thomas abstracts.
