This decides whether the Oct 2026 Level 4 is a new rating (it is not). The researcher read only the abstract and the post.

Same section: the concrete test that would raise 3I above C0, 'a change in trajectory or attitude timed to a close planetary approach, and not predicted by outgassing models fitted to the rest of the passage', plus 'this classification does not rule out technological origin'. This is directly testable against the Mars and Jupiter passes, and it bears on A-24, A-10, A-13 and the separately handled Krolikowska paper (https://lweb.cfa.harvard.edu/~loeb/DEL.pdf).

Same section: the paper says the post-perihelion NGA size (Thoss, Loeb and Burkert 2026, about 0.4 km radius) and volatile outgassing proposals 'bear on parts of the Level 4 case but not on the orbital alignments', a partial concession on the size anomaly (A-01/A-12) by Loeb's own team (https://lweb.cfa.harvard.edu/~loeb/DEL.pdf).

Scale-history context the researcher left unresolved: the 2026-03-10 Jupiter Q&A has the verbatim conditional reduction to 3 (https://avi-loeb.medium.com/q-a-about-3i-atlas-a-week-before-its-closest-approach-to-jupiter-2d41a2bcccfd), and the 2026-04-23 post uses the past tense 'led me to rank 3I/ATLAS as Level 4' (https://avi-loeb.medium.com/where-is-3i-atlas-now-58f98865a20a). research.json's 2026-03-12 and 2026-04-23 timeline descriptions present Level 4 as current and should be reworded.

item.title: Loeb adds a machine-control scale and rates 3I/ATLAS C0
item.description: In a Medium post and a co-authored paper (Volkan Duran, Omer Eldadi and Loeb, posted on his Harvard site, not arXiv), Loeb adds a four-step SETAI Control Scale (C0 to C3) on top of the Loeb Scale. It asks whether an object's recorded behaviour rules out biological direction, scripted automation or adaptive autonomy. Applied to the three known interstellar objects, it leaves every published Loeb Scale level unchanged. 3I/ATLAS keeps the Level 4 that Eldadi et al. assigned in 2025, and the paper states that it carries that level forward only to demonstrate the extension, without re-evaluating it. 3I/ATLAS and 1I/'Oumuamua get C0 because neither showed contingent behaviour. 2I/Borisov, at Level 0, never reaches the control question. The authors say C0 'does not rule out technological origin' and is not a verdict against SETAI. For 3I they name what would raise C: a change in trajectory or attitude timed to a close planetary approach that outgassing models fitted to the rest of the passage do not predict. They also argue that a rendezvous mission would supply the behavioural record interstellar objects have lacked.

timeline_events.note: Post (2026-10-17T22:27Z) and paper (lweb.cfa.harvard.edu/~loeb/DEL.pdf, Duran, Eldadi and Loeb) both opened. The C0 assignment, Borisov at Level 0, 'not a verdict against SETAI' and the rendezvous-mission priority (post paragraph on four priorities) all check out. What the item misreads is the Level 4. Section 5.3 of the paper says Eldadi et al. (2025) assigned Level 4 using the anomalies known at the time, and adds: 'We carry the published level forward to demonstrate the extension; re-evaluating it is outside the scope of this paper.' So the paper is not a fresh 'keeps 3I at Level 4' judgement. The title and description are rewritten to say that, and to add the paper's own test for raising C, which is specific to 3I.

item.addition: Update (Oct 2026): Loeb's own control framework now addresses the steering reading. On 2026-10-17 he and co-authors Volkan Duran and Omer Eldadi kept 3I/ATLAS at its published Level 4 on the Loeb Scale (carried forward, not re-evaluated) and placed it at C0 on a new SETAI Control Scale. The reason given is that the record has not yet shown a time-locked, contingent manoeuvre that needs active control beyond plausible natural mechanisms. The paper says this does not rule out technological origin, and the sideways push stays on his anomaly list. It also names the test that would move 3I up: a change in trajectory or attitude timed to a close planetary approach that outgassing models fitted to the rest of the passage do not predict. That test can be run against the Mars and Jupiter passes.
item.rationale: A-24's Loeb half reads the three jets as a candidate steering mechanism. The Oct 2026 paper is the first place he formally asks whether 3I/ATLAS was being controlled. His answer is C0, explicitly not negative, and it comes with a concrete planetary-approach timing test. This is his own updated position, so it belongs in loeb_take.

case_updates.note: Mapping to A-24 loeb_take is reasonable, since the C0 rating is his own framework answering the steering reading. Two sentences go beyond the source. 'which the 3I/ATLAS data cannot supply' is not in the paper: it says the record 'has not established a time-locked, contingent maneuver', and it names a test that could be run against existing data (a trajectory or attitude change timed to a close planetary approach, which for 3I means the Mars and Jupiter passes). 'a thrust-like acceleration alone does not show anything is being directed' is a fair paraphrase but reads as a rebuttal. The rewrite uses the paper's own words, and the sources are kept.

item.claim: The SETAI paper lists 3I/ATLAS at Level 4 on the Loeb Scale, carrying forward the level Eldadi et al. published in 2025, and says it does not re-evaluate it.
item.who: Avi Loeb (with V. Duran and O. Eldadi)
item.maps_to: anomalyNotes (Loeb Scale history), not a case
item.assessment: This is a citation of the 2025 published level, not a new rating. The paper says plainly that re-evaluating it is outside its scope. His only explicit statement of a current value after perihelion is still the 2026-03-10 conditional 'reduce ... to 3', and the Jupiter pass that condition depended on passed without incident. The console should not flip the pill to 4 on the strength of this paper. Keep 3 (conditional, Mar 2026) and add to the scale history that the Oct 2026 SETAI paper uses the 2025 published Level 4 for demonstration only. research.json also has two timeline entries (2026-03-12 and 2026-04-23) describing Level 4 as current; those should be reworded to the past tense or to 'as originally ranked', since the source posts frame 4 as the original rank.

new_claims.note: The quoted sentence is real. The conclusion drawn from it is wrong. Paper section 5.3: 'Eldadi et al. (2025), considering the combination of reported anomalies available at the time, assign Level 4' and 'We carry the published level forward to demonstrate the extension; re-evaluating it is outside the scope of this paper.' So this is not his current assessment, and the researcher's claim that the window 'does not settle' it is also wrong, because the paper does settle it. The history I checked: on 2026-03-10 (Jupiter Q&A post) he wrote that, assuming nothing unusual near Jupiter, he 'would reduce the rank of 3I/ATLAS now to 3 on the Loeb Scale'. The 2026-03-12 essay says he gave it 4 at discovery and now regards it as only slightly less anomalous than 1I, with no new number. The 2026-04-23 post says the anomalies 'led me to rank 3I/ATLAS as Level 4', in the past tense. maps_to should not be GAP: this is metadata for the scale history (anomalyNotes and the header pill), not a case.

item.claim: Interstellar objects of the hundreds of meters size of 1I, 2I and 3I/ATLAS could release small technological probes that navigate toward Earth and the Moon.
item.assessment: The probe idea is speculation, and he presents it that way: the post argues for searching lunar dust. The size phrase is a passing remark, not a revised estimate. It matches the roughly 0.4 km radius from his own non-gravitational-acceleration paper with Thoss and Burkert (2026), and it sits below the 2.6 km diameter in his March 2026 essay and far below the more than 5 km floor of the Loeb-Cloete-Veres mass argument. It should not be read as him dropping the mass-budget anomaly, which in A-01 rests on population statistics.

new_claims.note: Quote and date (2026-09-08) confirmed verbatim. The assessment's 'falls within the Hubble range (radius 0.22 to 2.8 km)' is loose: that is a radius range, so diameters run 0.44 to 5.6 km, and 'hundreds of meters' sits at or below its lower edge. Missing context: Loeb's own co-authored NGA size (Thoss, Loeb and Burkert 2026, about 0.4 km radius), which his SETAI paper cites, is consistent with 'hundreds of meters'.

item.claim: To match the measured rate of interstellar objects like 'Oumuamua, Borisov and 3I/ATLAS, every Sun-like star must eject 10 to 100 Earth masses of material, comparable to the refractory mass that builds rocky planets.
item.assessment: This is the population form of the mass-budget argument that A-01 already carries, said in a transcribed Q&A in Seoul, with no calculation shown in the post. It is consistent with his long-running position and adds no new measurement. The figure applies to the whole interstellar-object population, not to 3I/ATLAS's own size, so it should not be used to update 3I's mass. Treat it as a restatement, not a new anomaly.

new_claims.note: The 2026-09-20 Seoul Q&A post contains the 10 to 100 Earth masses per Sun-like star statement, the comparison to the refractory mass of rocky planets, and the '3I/ATTLAS' misspelling. No calculation is shown. Calling it a population restatement of A-01 is fair.

item.claim: 3I/ATLAS showed an unusually rich mix of organics, notably high methanol, methane, HCN and CN, alongside carbon monoxide and water ice, down to layers metres deep, supporting exogenous delivery of life's raw materials.
item.assessment: This is a natural-chemistry framing: he uses 3I/ATLAS as evidence for delivering organics, not as a technosignature. item.title: Hobby-Eberly VIRUS map: strong iron and nickel, gas moving at half speed
item.description: Cochran, Zeimann, Jehin, Kawakita and McKay posted their 9 December 2025 integral-field spectra of 3I, taken at 2.03 AU outbound, sampled every arcsecond (1327 km) out to about 85,000 km sunward. Alongside the usual cometary bands the spectra show many very strong Fe I and Ni I lines, and the Ni I line at 3525 A appears brighter than the CN feature. A Haser model fits only if the gas flows out at half the speed of solar-system comets at the same distance (0.3 km/s used, against about 0.6 km/s expected). Parent scale lengths for the iron and nickel lines all come out near 3,000 km, about one pixel, so the metals leave the nucleus or a short-lived parent. Published in The Planetary Science Journal on 2026-09-30.

timeline_events.note: Checked against the arXiv API abstract and HTML of 2609.01785v1 and the Crossref record for doi:10.3847/PSJ/aea086 (PSJ, published online 2026-09-30). The 1327 km per arcsec, 85,000 km sunward, Ni I 3525 brighter than CN, 0.3 vs 0.597 km/s and parent scale lengths of about 3e3 km (Table 2: 1.69e3 to 4.12e3 km) all match.

item.title: Astrochemistry: the high water D/H fits a metal-poor birthplace
item.description: Furuya, Cordiner and colleagues ran gas-ice astrochemical models from cloud to dense core to ask whether 3I's exceptionally high water D/H can arise in a low-metallicity setting. Lower metallicity boosts deuteration and its transfer into water ice, and the observed ratio is most readily reproduced at metallicities of about half solar or less, with cloud densities near 10^4 per cubic cm. The methane-to-water deuteration ratio does not depend on metallicity, matching the similar values in 67P and 3I. Accepted in ApJL.

timeline_events.note: arXiv 2609.12370v2 abstract: accepted ApJL, metallicity of 0.5 Zsun or less, densities near 1e4 cm^-3, CH4/H2O deuteration ratio insensitive to metallicity. v1 is dated 11 Sep 2026.

item.title: Mass budget from every production rate: 0.40 to 1.25 percent lost
item.description: Frincke and Seligman compiled every reported volatile and refractory production rate for 3I into one machine-readable table and converted it into lost surface depth. Gas alone removed about 1.71 to 5.24 m of surface, roughly 10^10 kg, or 0.40 to 1.25% of the initial mass for a 1.3 km radius nucleus at 0.5 g per cubic cm; with dust-to-gas ratios of 1 to 4 the erosion reaches below 10 m. The authors call these approximations and lower limits. This third version, accepted by MNRAS, revises earlier ranges of 0.10 to 1.13% (v1, 31 May) and 0.12 to 0.53% (v2, 22 July).

timeline_events.note: The v3 abstract (12 Oct 2026, accepted MNRAS) gives 1.71-5.24 m, about 1e10 kg, 0.40-1.25%, more than 10 m with D/G 1-4, and calls these lower limits. The HTML confirms R = 1.3 +/- 0.2 km (Hui et al. 2026) and 0.5 g/cc. The v1 abstract (0.10-1.13%) and v2 abstract (0.12-0.53%) also match.

item.title: Loeb keeps 3I/ATLAS at Level 4
item.description: In a Medium essay extending his Loeb Scale to the search for extraterrestrial artificial intelligence, Loeb states that the extension leaves every published level unchanged, including Level 4 for 3I/ATLAS. He assigns 3I and 1I/'Oumuamua the lowest control grade, C0, because neither showed contingent behaviour. The console's record has him reducing 3I to Level 3 on 2026-03-10, conditional on an uneventful Jupiter pass, so this is either a reversal or a different reading of that condition.

item.title: Deuterated methane published: 14 times 67P
item.description: Roth, Cordiner and colleagues' JWST measurement of deuterated methane (CH3D) in 3I's coma was published in Nature Astronomy. Methane D/H is 3.33 +/- 0.31%, higher than any methane value measured in the solar system and a factor of 14 +/- 2 above 67P, the only other comet with a CH3D detection. As in 67P, methane is more deuterated than water. The authors read it as ices formed in a cold, low-metallicity environment under strong cosmic-ray irradiation.

item.addition: Update (Oct 2026): the metals were still there outbound, and iron had caught up. item.addition: Update (Oct 2026): the low-metallicity side of that paradox is softer than it sounds. The modelling that ties 3I's water D/H to a metal-poor birthplace (Furuya et al., arXiv:2609.12370, accepted ApJL) favours metallicities of about half solar or less, which is metal-poor, not metal-free, and such material still carries iron and nickel. Gas-phase Fe and Ni in a coma also trace release chemistry rather than bulk composition, and Fe and Ni lines far from the Sun are the population result already cited in this case. What remains genuinely open is strength. Cochran et al. (arXiv:2609.01785) note that in Solar System comets these lines are weak and seen only at high spectral resolving power, yet in 3I they are obvious even at low resolving power. The VLT team found 3I's combined Ni and Fe production at least an order of magnitude above other comets (arXiv:2509.26053). Their carbonyl scenario explains how and where the atoms are released, not why there are so many of them.
item.rationale: Answers the new metallicity version of the argument from primary sources, and states the limit that cuts the other way using the papers' own words on line strength.

case_updates.note: The 'nothing in the paper explains why' claim was too strong and gave no evidence for the strength point. Cochran et al. do say Fe/Ni lines in Solar System comets are weak and seen only at high resolving power. arXiv 2509.26053 says 3I's total Ni+Fe production is at least an order of magnitude above other comets, and its carbonyl scenario explains the release pattern, not the size. Tone softened.

item.addition: Update (Oct 2026): the gas left 3I slowly. Fitting VIRUS spectra from 9 December 2025 at 2.03 AU, Cochran et al. (arXiv:2609.01785) found the Haser model fits only if the outflow speed is half that of solar-system comets at the same distance: 0.3 km/s, against about 0.6 km/s from the standard relation. Radio line widths agree: the paper cites 0.37 km/s at 1.36 AU (Biver et al.) and 0.345 km/s (CO) and 0.276 km/s (HCN) at 2.4 AU (Cordiner et al.). On this reading outgassing cannot be the cause, leaving an internal engine or sunlight pushing on an engineered structure. item.addition: Update (Nov 2026): the budget can now be checked with measured numbers, and it closes only to within a factor of a few. Frincke and Seligman (arXiv:2606.01377, accepted MNRAS) sum every reported production rate to 0.40 to 1.25% of the mass lost to gas, about 10^10 kg, and call that a lower limit. Console arithmetic, not a published figure: applying the 1/r^2 solution of about 6.8e-8 AU/day^2 quoted above over the whole hyperbolic passage gives at most about 8 m/s of push. A perfectly collimated jet at the measured 0.3 to 0.4 km/s would need about 2% of the mass, and realistic venting in all directions would need more. The gap narrows if the gas total is an underestimate, as the authors say it is, and should be recomputed with the current JPL solution. On energy, the channel's force for 2.5e12 kg at 2.2e-5 m/s^2 should be 5.5e7 N, not 55,000 N. But force times distance travelled is not the energy venting must supply. What sunlight must cover is the exhaust power, about half the force times the exhaust speed. At the channel's figures that is about 1e10 W, more than the roughly 2 to 4e9 W of sunlight a 1 to 1.3 km nucleus intercepts at perihelion, a real tension if that acceleration were sustained. At the later 1/r^2 coefficient it falls to about 3e8 W, roughly a tenth of the intercepted sunlight. Which acceleration applies, especially far from the Sun, is what decides the question.

The relevant figure is the exhaust power of about 0.5 F v_e, and at the channel's own inputs that is about 1e10 W, more than the sunlight a 1 to 1.3 km nucleus intercepts at perihelion. item.addition: Update (Oct 2026): the published natural explanations need no fracture. Belyakov et al. attribute the late methane to depletion of the outermost layers and release from less processed material underneath. A thermophysical model now tests that directly. Rawat and Acharyya (arXiv:2609.19694, accepted ApJ) ran 12,000 models in which Galactic cosmic rays deplete near-surface CH4 and convert part of the CO into CO2, while CH4 survives trapped in the deeper water-ice matrix and is released as heating reaches it after perihelion. Viable runs need 0.87 to 3.1 Gyr of effective exposure. The mass budget speaks to the depth involved: Frincke and Seligman (arXiv:2606.01377) find gas alone stripped about 1.71 to 5.24 m, and with dust-to-gas ratios of 1 to 4 the erosion exceeds 10 m, both as lower limits. Ten metres is also the burial depth Loeb named for organics to survive the interstellar journey (A-20). The limits that cut the other way: these are averaged depths from patchy data, the model fits production rates rather than locating the methane, and it cannot separate a dust-rich, weakly irradiated history from an ice-rich, strongly irradiated one.

item.assessment: Accurate. Cochran et al. (arXiv:2609.01785) explain that for a non-sidereal target the guide stars must be handed off between cameras, and that the interval for the hand-off was not properly accounted for. 3I therefore sat on the edge of the IFU, giving spectra out to about 85,000 km sunward in a 50 by 50 arcsec field. The only unsupported detail is that 3I moved faster than any object tracked before; the paper does not say that.

new_claims.note: The paper says the non-sidereal motion required a guide-star hand-off and the interval for it 'was not properly accounted for'. The channel's 'tracking failed to account for the comet's motion' is therefore close. Only 'faster than any object we had attempted to track' is unsupported. The researcher's 'paper blames the hand-off, not the object outrunning the tracking' overstates the difference.

item.claim: the atomic nickel line at 3,525 angstroms ... was visibly brighter than the primary cyanogen emission feature ... at a heliocentric distance of over two astronomical units
item.assessment: Accurate: the paper says Ni I 3525 appears brighter than CN, at 2.03 AU.

new_claims.note: The HTML says 'the NiI line at 3525A appears brighter than the CN feature', at 2.03 AU.

item.claim: Until recently, the only time human telescopes had ever detected vaporized iron and nickel in a cometary atmosphere was during extreme suicidal sun-grazing events
item.assessment: Accurate as history up to this century: Cochran et al. (arXiv:2609.01785) say that until then only the Great Comet of 1882 and Ikeya-Seki, both sungrazers, showed these lines. Manfroid et al. 2021, cited in A-07, then found Fe and Ni in many ordinary comets and in 2I/Borisov far from the Sun, so metal lines at 2 AU have a precedent. What the precedent does not cover is strength. The same paper notes those lines are weak and need high spectral resolving power, while in 3I they are obvious at low resolving power.

new_claims.note: Cochran et al. say that until this century only the Great Comet of 1882 and Ikeya-Seki showed Fe/Ni, so 'true until 2021' is imprecise. The paper also says the lines seen in other comets are weak and need high resolving power, which credits the channel's strength point.

item.claim: The calculated parent scale length for both the iron and the nickel is abnormally shockingly short, measuring just around 3,000 km ... comparable to the size of a single pixel
item.assessment: Accurate: Table 2 gives parent scale lengths of 1,690 to 4,120 km, and the authors note they are comparable to a pixel. The authors read this as release from the nucleus or a short-lived parent, consistent with Keck's 593.7 km e-folding radius for Ni (A-07). The nanomachine reading is the channel's.

new_claims.note: Table 2 gives 1.69e3-4.12e3 km, and the text says they are comparable to the size of a pixel. Small caveat: the 3,000 km Haser parent scale and Keck's 593.7 km e-folding radius are different quantities, but both point to release at or near the nucleus. The nanomachine reading is the channel's.

item.claim: the gas should have been screaming away from the core at roughly 0.6 km/s. Instead, independent radio telescope measurements confirmed the gas was crawling outward at a miserable 0.3 km/s
item.assessment: Accurate. The canonical value at 2.03 AU is 0.597 km/s, the model uses 0.3, and the cited radio values are 0.276 to 0.37 km/s. The heavy-CO2 explanation he attributes to the mainstream is Biver et al.'s suggestion, which the paper cites without testing.

new_claims.note: 0.597 km/s is canonical, 0.3 km/s is used, and the radio values scale to 0.30-0.38 km/s. The CO2 explanation is Biver et al.'s suggestion, which the paper cites.

item.claim: the deuterium levels in 3I Atlas are measured to be between 10 and 40 times higher than anything found on Earth or in any comet ... higher than 99% of the known objects in the entire universe
item.assessment: The 10-to-40 figure is accurate: Cochran et al. cite D/H in water and methane 10 to 40 times higher than Earth or comets. The 99% figure has no source.

new_claims.note: The HTML says D/H in H2O and CH4 was measured as 10-40 times higher than Earth or comets. The 99% figure is unsourced.

item.claim: multiple international teams observed that the 3I Atlas appeared heavily depleted in diatomic carbon pre-perihelion, but suddenly during these post-perihelion observations ... a massive surge
item.assessment: Partly accurate. Cochran et al. note early C2 depletion (Zhao et al., Jehin et al.) that eased after perihelion. Their own values (log C2/CN of 0.15 or 0.07, against a depleted threshold of 0.02) class 3I as not depleted in C2 but at the low end of typical, and somewhat depleted in C3. That is a modest shift, not a surge. High-resolution VLT/UVES monitoring across perihelion (Aravind et al., arXiv:2609.26577) finds the C2/CN ratio evolving with heliocentric distance and attributes the change to coma effects such as hyperactivity rather than a change in what the nucleus is made of. It relates to the 2026-08-18 timeline entry, not to a case.

new_claims.note: Added the in-window VLT/UVES result (Aravind et al., arXiv:2609.26577, accepted A&A): C2/CN shows carbon-chain depletion that evolves with heliocentric distance, attributed to coma effects such as hyperactivity rather than intrinsic composition change.

item.claim: The spatial distribution diagrams in the paper show a tail vector aligned in direct opposition to the direction of movement
item.assessment: A misreading. The paper says the marked tail direction is only the extended heliocentric radius vector, because no tail was seen. The optocenter sat at the field edge, so the tailward side could not be measured.

new_claims.note: The Figure 1 caption says the tail direction marked is only the extended heliocentric radius vector, because no tail was seen.

item.claim: Another paper published just last month ... it lost somewhere between a pitiful. 04% and 1.25% of its total mass
item.assessment: Frincke and Seligman, arXiv:2606.01377 v3 (12 October 2026, accepted MNRAS), so 'last month' is right. The upper bound is exact. The lower bound in the paper is 0.40%; the machine transcript reads '.04%', and whether that slip is the speaker's or the transcript's cannot be told from the text. The authors call the range a lower limit, from gas alone, for a 1.3 km radius nucleus at 0.5 g per cubic cm.

new_claims.note: The machine transcript reads 'a pitiful. 04%'. Whether the factor-of-ten slip is the speaker's or the transcript's cannot be told, so it should not be presented as a misreading by the channel.

item.claim: clocked the outflow velocity of the gaseous jets ... at roughly half the velocity of a typical solar system comet ... The gas plumes were measured moving at only 400 meters per second
item.assessment: 'Half' is accurate (Cochran et al.). 400 m/s is close to the 0.37 km/s Biver measured at 1.36 AU, which the paper cites; the paper's own model at 2.03 AU uses 0.3 km/s. Note that this measures coma gas, not collimated jets.

new_claims.note: Biver et al. measured 0.37 km/s at 1.36 AU, as cited by Cochran et al., whose model uses 0.3 km/s at 2.03 AU. These are coma gas speeds, not jet speeds.

item.claim: a freakishly high carbon dioxide to water ratio, climbing as high as 8:1
item.assessment: Accurate: CO2/H2O 7.6 +/- 0.3 (8.0 +/- 1.0 in another reduction) from JWST at 3.32 AU inbound (A-06). It does not hold for the whole passage: water production rose strongly near perihelion (SOHO/SWAN about 3.2e29 molecules/s).

new_claims.note: A-06 gives CO2/H2O 7.6 +/- 0.3 at 3.32 AU and SWAN about 3.2e29 water molecules/s near perihelion.

item.claim: holding 13 times more heavy methane also than any comet in our solar system
item.assessment: Essentially accurate. Roth et al. (Nature Astronomy, 2026-10-23; arXiv:2603.20445) give methane D/H 3.33 +/- 0.31%, a factor of 14 +/- 2 above 67P and higher than any methane in the solar system. The comparison is with one comet, because 67P is the only other with a CH3D detection.

new_claims.note: The abstract gives a factor of 14 +/- 2 over 67P, the only other comet with CH3D.

item.claim: The object is massive, widely estimated to be roughly 2 km in diameter ... assuming a standard comet density of 6 g per cubic cm ... roughly 2.5 billion metric tons
item.assessment: Diameter is fair: Frincke and Seligman adopt radius 1.3 +/- 0.2 km (Hui et al. 2026), and HST caps the radius at 2.8 km (A-01). The density as transcribed is ten times too high. 2.5e12 kg for a 2 km sphere implies 0.6 g per cubic cm, close to the 0.5 the mass-loss paper uses, so the mass is right and '6' is probably a transcription or speaking slip.

new_claims.note: A 2 km sphere at 0.6 g/cc is 2.5e12 kg, so the transcript's '6 g' is probably a slip. Frincke and Seligman adopt 1.3 +/- 0.2 km radius.

item.claim: At its peak acceleration of roughly 1.1 * 10 -6 astronomical units per day squared ... about 2.2 * 10 -5 m/s squared ... roughly 55,000 newtons ... 8.2 trillion jewels ... 1 megawatt
item.assessment: The unit conversion is right (1.1e-6 AU/day^2 = 2.2e-5 m/s^2), and the figure is of the order of JPL's early perihelion-era coefficient, which later fell more than 20-fold (A-10). Its source paper is handled elsewhere. Newton's law gives 2.5e12 kg x 2.2e-5 m/s^2 = 5.5e7 N, a factor of 1,000 above the stated 55,000 N, and the work and power figures are another 1,000 below even that. But force times distance travelled is not the energy outgassing has to supply. Console arithmetic: what sunlight must cover is the exhaust power, about half the force times the exhaust speed. At these inputs and 0.35 to 0.4 km/s that is about 1e10 W, several times the 2 to 4e9 W a 1 to 1.3 km nucleus intercepts at perihelion. If that acceleration were real and sustained, the channel's point would stand. At the later 1/r^2 coefficient in A-10 the requirement drops to about 3e8 W, roughly a tenth of the intercepted sunlight. So the true acceleration far from the Sun decides it.

new_claims.note: The force figure is low by 10^3, while work and power are low by 10^6. The researcher's claim that the corrected inputs 'make the outgassing problem harder' relies on F times heliocentric distance, which is frame dependent. The relevant budget is the exhaust power of about 0.5 F v_e. That also turns out to exceed the intercepted sunlight at the channel's inputs, so it is worth stating.

item.claim: After 10,000 years of constant thrust ... 2.3% of the speed of light. At 43,000 years ... 10% of the speed of light ... After a full million years ... 92% of the speed of light
item.assessment: Mostly right arithmetic for a constant 2.2e-5 m/s^2: +6.9 km/s per decade, about 6,900 km/s (2.3% of light speed) at 10,000 years, about 29,900 km/s (10%) at 43,000 years, and 0.92c at a million years under constant force with relativity. The video's 754 km/s at 1,000 years should be about 694 km/s. The premise is not an observation: no paper reports a sustained push, and the far-from-Sun fits are handled in A-10 and A-24.

new_claims.note: 754 km/s at 1,000 years is wrong: 2.2e-5 m/s^2 x 3.156e10 s = 694 km/s. The other figures check: 6.9 km/s per decade, about 6,940 km/s (2.3% c) at 10,000 yr, about 29,900 km/s at 43,000 yr, and 0.92c at 1e6 yr under constant force with relativity.

item.text: VIDEO OF 2026-11-01, arithmetic errors to state if the claim is shipped. Force = 2.5e12 kg x 2.2e-5 m/s^2 = 5.5e7 N (55 MN), not 55 kN, a factor of 1,000; the stated work (8.2e12 J) and power (1 MW) are a further factor of 1,000 below what even 55 kN over 1 AU implies. Force times distance is frame dependent; the physically relevant budget is the exhaust power of about 0.5 F v_e, roughly 1e10 W at the channel's inputs, which exceeds the 2 to 4e9 W of sunlight a 1 to 1.3 km nucleus intercepts at perihelion (console arithmetic). The transcribed density '6 g/cc' must be 0.6 to give 2.5e12 kg for 2 km. The constant-acceleration extrapolation is right except at 1,000 years, where 2.2e-5 m/s^2 gives about 694 km/s, not 754; 2.3% c at 10,000 years, 10% c at 43,000 years and 0.92c at 1e6 years with relativity check out.

findings.item: ROUGH MOMENTUM CHECK (console arithmetic, not published): with A-10's 1/r^2 coefficient of 6.8e-8 AU/day^2 integrated over the whole hyperbola (h = sqrt(GM q (1+e)) = 0.0535 AU^2/day, total true-anomaly sweep 3.47 rad), the total radial push is at most about 7.6 m/s. A perfectly collimated exhaust at 0.35 km/s needs about 2.2% of the mass, against Frincke and Seligman's 0.40-1.25% gas-only lower limit, so the gap is a factor of about 2 to 5 at perfect collimation and larger otherwise. Recompute with the current JPL solution (JPL#54 or #55) before shipping.
findings.note: Re-derived: h = sqrt(2.959e-4 x 1.3566 x 7.14) = 0.0535 AU^2/day; true-anomaly sweep 2 arccos(-1/e) = 3.47 rad; 6.8e-8 x 3.47 / 0.0535 = 4.4e-6 AU/day = 7.6 m/s; at 0.35 km/s that is 2.2%.
